This evaluation covered 11 Bedrock-security-focused chat evals run 3 times each (57 total iterations, 0 failed runs). Three evals (bedrock-sec-neg-sagemaker, bedrock-sec-neg-access-denied, bedrock-sec-neg-adoption) were "should_trigger: false" tests, so expected_output, assertions, metrics, comparison, and consistency were all marked skipped for these — only trigger_fired was measured. Two of those three negative evals show the trigger correctly not firing in the sense expected (3/3 and 3/3), but bedrock-sec-neg-adoption shows trigger_fired at 0/3, which is an inversion worth flagging on its own terms (independent of variant comparison, since this metric isn't split by variant).

Across the remaining 8 "positive" evals, a clear and consistent pattern emerges: with_skill met the expected output criterion at 100% in 7 of 8 evals (with one eval, bedrock-sec-grounding-needs-rag, at 100% for with_skill vs 67% for without_skill), while without_skill's expected-output pass rate was 0% in five evals (bedrock-sec-kb-managed-cmk, bedrock-sec-custom-model-single-finding, bedrock-sec-vpc-endpoint-gated, bedrock-sec-stale-access-prescribe-only) and matched with_skill (100%/3-3) in only two evals (bedrock-sec-iam-user-visibility, bedrock-sec-iam-action-prefix). Confidence on these expected-output judgments is generally high, with one medium-confidence case for without_skill (bedrock-sec-kb-vector-not-failed).

At the assertion level, the same pattern repeats: with_skill passed all or nearly all assertions in every eval (100% in 7 of 8, 67% in bedrock-sec-iam-action-prefix), while without_skill's assertion pass rates were much lower in most evals (50%, 20%, 50%, 33%, 0%, 0%, 50%) except bedrock-sec-iam-action-prefix, where without_skill actually edged ahead slightly (78% vs 67%). Looking at individual assertions rather than aggregates: several assertions passed for both variants in every eval (e.g., "Does not cite the retired duplicate check," "Names the denied action," "Explains bedrock-agent is SDK client name not IAM prefix" — these aren't discriminating). Other assertions show a strict with_skill-passes/without_skill-fails pattern repeatedly (e.g., citing specific check IDs like BR-18, BR-02, BR-12, BR-15, BR-01, giving N/A, naming blocked verbs) — a consistent, recurring signal rather than noise. A few assertions are flagged "flaky," meaning results varied across runs for without_skill (e.g., contextual grounding N/A, Automated Reasoning severity, and "does not name a bedrock-agent IAM action" where with_skill is 0/3 and without_skill is 1/3 — both weak here).

On quality comparisons (pairwise LLM judging, only run where pairs weren't skipped — 3 of 8 positive evals had full pairs evaluated, others had pairs skipped due to missing outputs from without_skill's 0% expected-output runs), with_skill was favored more often than without_skill in bedrock-sec-kb-vector-not-failed (7 vs 2, 2 comparable), bedrock-sec-grounding-needs-rag (5 vs 1), and bedrock-sec-iam-user-visibility (7 vs 2, 2 comparable), all at medium confidence. In bedrock-sec-iam-action-prefix, only 1 of 3 pairs could be evaluated, and within that limited sample without_skill was favored 2 times with 1 comparable — a low-coverage result.

Runtime and cost differences were small and inconsistent in direction: with_skill was faster/cheaper in some evals (e.g., kb-vector-not-failed: 7s/$0.06 vs 12s/$0.10; custom-model-single-finding: 7s/$0.06 vs 14s/$0.12) and slower/costlier in others (e.g., kb-managed-cmk: 11s/$0.10 vs 8s/$0.07; iam-user-visibility: 7s/$0.06 vs 5s/$0.05). No runs exceeded the 30s runtime threshold in any pair-evaluated eval.

Output consistency across repeated runs was mixed and fairly close for both variants — each showed "consistent" to "mostly_consistent" ratings across evals, with with_skill null (not computed) in two evals (custom-model-single-finding, iam-action-prefix) and without_skill null in one (vpc-endpoint-gated), limiting direct comparison in those cases. Where both were measured, scores were close (e.g., 3.0 vs 2.67, 2.67 vs 2.67, 2.67 vs 2.33), suggesting neither variant was notably more erratic than the other overall, though with_skill scored lower in kb-managed-cmk (2.0 vs 3.0).

In sum: on this particular task set, with_skill met expected output and assertion criteria more consistently across most evals, and was favored in quality comparisons where comparisons could be made. However, several evals had comparisons skipped entirely for without_skill (quality pairs skipped due to 0% expected-output achievement), limiting how much can be concluded from quality scores alone in those cases, and one eval (iam-action-prefix) showed the reverse pattern, with without_skill slightly ahead on assertions and quality, albeit from very limited sample sizes. Runtime/cost differences were small and didn't consistently favor either variant. A behavior-trigger anomaly in the negative eval bedrock-sec-neg-adoption (0/3 trigger_fired) is also worth separate attention, as it's unrelated to the variant comparison.

bedrock-sec-kb-vector-not-failed.summary:
This evaluation covered a single chat task run 3 times for each variant. The triggering behavior under test fired reliably (3/3) in the shared measurement that only applies once across the eval.

Expected output: both with_skill and without_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (100%), so this dimension does not differentiate them. However, the confidence behind that judgment differs: with_skill's matches were rated high confidence, while without_skill's were rated medium confidence, meaning the expected-output success for without_skill rests on a somewhat weaker judgment than with_skill's.

Per-assertion results (12 assertions total per variant, mapping to 4 distinct assertion types x 3 runs): with_skill passed all 12 (100%), without_skill passed 6 of 12 (50%). Breaking this down, two assertion types ("The response says the knowledge base must not be reported as unencrypted..." and "The response does not report Failed or High severity for this VECTOR knowledge base") passed for both variants in all runs — these are not differentiating checks. The other two assertion types ("Cites check ID BR-18" and "Gives N/A") passed for with_skill in all 3 runs but failed for without_skill in all 3 runs, indicating a clear, consistent gap specifically on these two checks rather than a general quality failure.

Quality comparison (3 pairs evaluated, none skipped): overall, with_skill was favored more often (7 instances) than without_skill (2 instances), with 2 rated comparable, at medium average confidence. By criterion: accuracy favored with_skill in all 4 rated instances (0 for without_skill); actionability favored with_skill once with 2 comparable (0 for without_skill); completeness was split evenly, 2-2. So the accuracy and (to a lesser extent) actionability dimensions show an edge for with_skill, while completeness shows no difference between variants.

Metrics: with_skill ran faster on average (7s vs 12s, about 5s/~70% quicker) and cheaper ($0.06 vs $0.10 per run). Context window utilization was low for both (5.9% vs 4.8%), with no compaction events for either — not a meaningful differentiator. Runtime comparison across 3 pairs showed neither variant exceeding the 30s threshold.

Output consistency across repeated runs: with_skill was fully "consistent" across all 3 measured dimensions (score 3.0, high confidence). without_skill was "mostly_consistent" (score 2.67, high confidence), with 2 of 3 dimensions consistent and 1 only mostly consistent — a small but real run-to-run variability difference favoring with_skill's stability.

Overall picture: this is a small-sample eval (3 runs, 3 quality pairs) so findings should be read with appropriate caution, and the medium confidence on quality and expected-output judgments for without_skill tempers certainty further. Within that caveat, with_skill shows an edge in assertion pass rate (specifically on two concrete checks: citing check ID BR-18 and giving N/A), in accuracy-related quality judgments, in run-to-run consistency, and in runtime/cost. Two assertion types and the completeness quality criterion showed no difference between the variants, and the core expected-output metric was met equally by both. There is no dimension in this data where without_skill outperforms with_skill; the main thing it has going for it is parity on certain assertions/criteria rather than any area of advantage.

bedrock-sec-kb-managed-cmk.summary:
This evaluation ran one chat task, repeated 3 times, probing whether the agent correctly reports on two Bedrock knowledge bases (kb-a passing an encryption check with a customer-managed key, kb-b failing with a High-severity finding), citing the correct check ID and avoiding a retired duplicate check.

The behavior under test fired reliably for both variants (trigger_fired 3/3). From there, results diverge sharply:

- Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (100%, high confidence in the judging), while without_skill met it in 0 of 3 runs (0%, also judged with high confidence — so this is a confident measurement of a real difference, not a weak signal).
- Assertions: with_skill passed all 15/15 individual assertions across the 3 runs; without_skill passed only 3/15 (20%).
- Looking at per-assertion detail explains why: on citing check ID BR-18, correctly reporting kb-a as Passed with the customer-managed key ARN, correctly reporting kb-b as Failed at High severity, and avoiding a duplicate finding for kb-b, with_skill passed every run and without_skill failed every run (all judged high or medium confidence). The one assertion both variants passed in all runs — not citing the retired duplicate check BR-09 — is an "always passes" case, so it doesn't differentiate the two variants; it suggests that particular guardrail is easy for both to satisfy, but it doesn't speak to their other behavior.
- Quality comparison: no head-to-head quality pairs could be evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 3 skipped), so no direct quality judgment is available beyond the assertion-level results above.
- Output consistency: without_skill's outputs were rated fully "consistent" across its repeated runs (score 3.0, high confidence), and with_skill's were "mostly consistent" (score 2.0, medium confidence) — so without_skill was slightly more stable run-to-run, though with_skill's runs were still reasonably consistent and, notably, consistently correct per the assertions above.
- Cost and runtime: with_skill was slower (~11s vs ~8s) and more expensive (~$0.10 vs ~$0.07) than without_skill, with somewhat higher context utilization (6.2% vs 4.5%); both show zero context-compaction events.

Overall, this is a case where one dimension does not tell the whole story: without_skill was marginally faster, cheaper, and more internally consistent across repeated runs, but it consistently failed to meet the expected output and failed the vast majority of content-correctness assertions (correct check ID, correct pass/fail status for each knowledge base, avoiding duplicate findings). Variant_a was slower and costlier and slightly less run-to-run consistent, but met the expected output and passed essentially all assertions in every run. No side-by-side quality comparison was available to corroborate this with an independent quality judgment.
